Schemas

A schema is a declaration of the shape and types of fields in an event payload. Schemas ensure data consistency as events flow through your pipelines, allow destinations to validate incoming data, and power IDE autocomplete and validation in transforms.

Why schemas matter

Without explicit schemas, a pipeline has no way to know whether an incoming event's payload matches what the destination expects. Schemas solve this by:

  • Validating — Rejecting events that don't match the declared shape before they reach a destination.
  • Documenting — Making it clear to other engineers what fields a pipeline carries and what types they have.
  • Enabling safety checks — Detecting schema drift (unplanned changes to event shape) as data sources evolve.
  • Powering transforms — In transform code, your IDE can autocomplete fields because it knows the schema.

Declaring a schema

Schemas are declared at the connector level, not at the pipeline level. A source connector declares the shape of events it emits; a destination connector declares the shape it expects to receive.

connector-schema.json json 
{
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "order_id",
      "type": "string",
      "required": true,
      "description": "Unique order identifier"
    },
    {
      "name": "amount_cents",
      "type": "integer",
      "required": true,
      "description": "Order total in cents"
    },
    {
      "name": "customer_id",
      "type": "string",
      "required": false
    },
    {
      "name": "tags",
      "type": "array",
      "items": { "type": "string" },
      "required": false
    }
  ]
}

Each field declares:

  • name — The field key as it appears in the event payload.
  • type — One of string, integer, number, boolean, object, array, or null.
  • required — Whether the field must be present in every event.
  • description (optional) — Human-readable explanation of what the field contains.

Validation during processing

When an event flows through a pipeline, Godzilla validates the payload against the source connector's declared schema. If validation fails:

  • The event is marked with a validation error.
  • It is not passed to transforms or the destination.
  • It is moved to the pipeline's dead-letter queue.

This prevents corrupted or malformed data from corrupting downstream systems. See Handling errors & retries to learn how to inspect and replay dead-lettered events.

Schema evolution

As your source systems evolve, you may need to add or change fields in a schema. Godzilla supports schema evolution through versioning:

Backward compatibility

When adding a new field to a source schema, make it optional (required: false) to avoid breaking existing pipelines. When removing a field, plan a deprecation period and alert connected destinations.

Connecting the dots

Schemas sit between Events and Connectors:

  • Events carry the actual data; schemas declare what shape that data should have.
  • Connectors (both source and destination) each have their own schema, defining what they emit and what they expect.
  • A transform can reshape event payloads before they reach a destination, allowing you to map between different connector schemas.

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

event.json json 
{
  "id": "evt_8f2c1a90",
  "type": "order.created",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z",
  "source": "connector_postgres_orders",
  "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 }
}

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
Ordering

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

Payload shape and validation

Every event carries a payload — the actual user data. To ensure payload consistency and enable validation, you declare the expected shape of a payload using a schema. Schemas let connectors validate incoming data and allow transform code to safely access fields with IDE autocomplete.

Learn how to declare and use schemas in the Schemas concept guide.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

Concepts

The three building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.

Start with Pipelines

Godzilla is built from three ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

Concept

Pipelines

Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.

 Concept

Connectors

Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.

 Concept

Events

The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.

 Concept

Schemas

How event payload shapes are declared and validated to ensure data consistency.

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Schemas declare the shape of event payloads, enabling validation and safety checks as data flows through. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.
